1:
The chapter opens on a paradox the witnesses are quick to name — a good king at the height of his prosperity making the worst alliance of his life. The reformed John Gill takes the notice of riches and honour "in abundance" as still increasing, and reads it as the very thing that moved Ahab to desire friendship and affinity with Jehoshaphat, to which the king of Judah agreed. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms that the words are repeated from 2 Chronicles 17:5, and finds in the match itself the measure of Judah's standing: that so powerful a monarch as Ahab should enter into so intimate a connection is proof of the high prosperity to which Jehoshaphat had attained. He fixes the affinity precisely — the marriage of Jehoshaphat's son Jehoram to Athaliah, daughter of Ahab and Jezebel, the union whose bitter fruit appears at 2 Chronicles 21:6 — and notes, against Zöckler, that the connecting vav is not adversative but consecutive. The wesleyan-arminian voices agree on the fact: Adam Clarke and John Wesley both read the affinity as Jehoram's marriage to Ahab's daughter.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns the verse into a sustained lament over that marriage. Here is Jehoshaphat growing greater, he says, but not growing wiser, else he would never have joined with Ahab, that degenerate Israelite who had sold himself to work wickedness. What good could he get by a man so bad, or do to a man so obstinately wicked — an idolater, a persecutor? This, Henry declares, was the worst match ever made by any of the house of David, and he wonders what Jehoshaphat could promise himself by it. Perhaps pride made the match, as it makes many: his religion forbade him to marry his son to a daughter of the heathen princes about him, on the ground of Deuteronomy 7:3, and having riches in abundance he thought it a disparagement to marry the prince to a subject — a king's daughter it must be, and therefore Ahab's, little considering that Jezebel was her mother. Others, Henry allows, think he did it in policy, hoping to unite the kingdoms in his son, while Ahab flattered him with hopes of an inheritance he never meant to give.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Ellicott fix the fact and its worldly logic — the prosperous king made a desirable ally; Henry exposes the folly beneath the splendour. Between them they set the note the whole chapter will sound: that abundant riches and honour, as Henry elsewhere warns, give large opportunities of doing good but are attended with many snares, and that the affinity struck here in prosperity will nearly cost Jehoshaphat his life on the field of Ramoth-gilead, and will in time bring Athaliah's murderous hand upon the seed royal of David.
2:
Some years after the marriage, Jehoshaphat goes down to Samaria, and the witnesses read the royal banquet that meets him there as a snare dressed as hospitality. The reformed John Gill notes the interval — two years, by the Syriac and Arabic versions, or the third year after the affinity was contracted. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the chronology: the parallel at 1 Kings 22:2 reads "in the third year," a date reckoned from the three years' truce between Syria and Israel, and from 1 Kings 22:51 we learn the visit fell in the sixteenth or seventeenth year of Jehoshaphat's reign, so that the marriage of Jehoram and Athaliah had preceded it by some eight or nine years. Where the older history gives the exact "third year," intelligible only against Ahab's earlier wars, the chronicler, his fellow grammatical-historical witness Keil and Delitzsch observes, exchanges it for the indefinite "certain years," abridging a note that would have needed the whole background of Ahab's reign to explain.

On the feast the two schools converge in suspicion. Ellicott reads the killing of sheep and oxen "in abundance" as no mere courtesy but part of a deliberate plan to secure Jehoshaphat's co-operation in the projected campaign; and the verb rendered "persuaded" he glosses as "incited" or "pricked on," the word used of provoking to evil, as when Satan "provoked" David to number Israel at 1 Chronicles 21:1. Keil likewise sets the banquet at the head of the whole enterprise: Ahab feasted the king and his people and "persuaded him to go up with him to Ramoth-gilead," the campaign whose origin, course, and fatal result for Ahab the chapter will unfold in agreement with the record in 1 Kings 22, differing only in its introduction.

The witnesses do not contend; they read a single scene with one mind. Gill dates the visit; Ellicott and Keil expose the diplomacy behind the plates and cups. The lavish table at Samaria is not friendship but strategy — the wheedling of an easy-natured neighbour into a war that was Ahab's own, and the "persuading" is the same dangerous art by which the strong draw the pliable into their designs. What looks like the honour done a guest is in truth the baiting of a trap, and the reader who has watched Ahab kill his oxen for Jehoshaphat is meant to remember, before the chapter closes, whose blood the day will require.
3:
"Wilt thou go with me to Ramoth-gilead?" — and Jehoshaphat's ready "I am as thou art, and my people as thy people" draws the witnesses to weigh both the disputed city and the too-easy consent. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes the geography and its grievance: Ramoth-gilead belonged of right to the Israelites but was now held by the king of Syria, and the whole of the chapter, he says, is explained at large in the notes on 1 Kings 22. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes that the verse is essentially the same as 1 Kings 22:4, from which point the two narratives practically coincide; "Ramoth," he explains, means "heights," a common name in so hilly a country. But he marks one telling change: the chronicler has disturbed the symmetry of the older text — where Kings has Jehoshaphat pledge "my people as thy people, my horses as thy horses" — in order to make the king of Judah express an apparently more definite assent, "we will be with thee in the war."

His fellow grammatical-historical witness Keil and Delitzsch simply sets the exchange in its place at the head of the consultation that follows, as Ahab, having won the pledge, gathers his prophets. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, however, hears in that pledge the peril of a good man's complaisance. "I am as thou art": some men's kindnesses, he warns, are as dangerous as their society is infectious. The feast Ahab made was designed only to wheedle Jehoshaphat into the expedition, for the kisses of an enemy are deceitful; and Henry cannot but ask with what face Ahab could beg the king of Judah's help to recover a city for himself, when Ramoth and all the cities of Israel belonged of right to Jehoshaphat as heir of the house of David, and Ahab's own title was usurped and precarious.

The witnesses do not divide over the fact, only over its wisdom. Clarke and Ellicott establish the city and the near-identity with Kings; Keil carries the scene forward; Henry reads in the swift consent the fault of an easy man who could not say no to a wicked ally. Between them they show a king of Judah lending his people, his horses, and his own royal person to a quarrel not his own, and pledging himself in words fuller than the older record dared — a generosity that will very nearly leave him dead in another man's war.
4:
Amid the martial enthusiasm one sober voice is raised — "Inquire, I pray thee, at the word of the LORD to day" — and the witnesses honour Jehoshaphat's instinct even while they lament his company. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes that the words stand exactly as 1 Kings 22:5, and would render the phrase more precisely "seek the word" of the LORD. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draw from the request one of the great practical lessons of the chapter, and in almost identical terms. It is the great duty of acknowledging God in all our ways and enquiring at his word, whatever we undertake; Jehoshaphat, Henry observes, was not willing to proceed till he had done this. And how is such enquiry to be made? By particular believing prayer, by an unbiased consultation of the scripture and of our own consciences, and by an observant regard to the hints of providence — so, Wesley echoes, we should do whatever we undertake.

Yet the witnesses will not let the good instinct excuse the bad alliance. Henry turns at once to the great danger of bad company even to good men: those who have more wisdom, grace, and resolution than others cannot be sure they will converse familiarly with wicked people and get no hurt by them. Jehoshaphat, in complaisance to Ahab, will presently sit in his robes patiently hearing false prophets speak lies in the name of the LORD, can scarcely find in his heart to reprove Ahab for hating a true prophet, and dares neither rebuke the false prophet who abuses the faithful seer nor oppose the king who imprisons him. Those who venture among the seats of the scornful, Henry warns, cannot come off without a great deal of guilt attaching at least to the omission of their duty, unless they have measures of wisdom and courage that few can pretend to.

The witnesses converge on a divided portrait. Ellicott secures the text; Henry and Wesley, of their kindred schools, hold together the honour and the hazard — that Jehoshaphat did well to seek the word of the LORD before he drew the sword, and did ill to seek it at the court of a man who hated that word. The verse becomes a mirror for every believer drawn into the undertakings of the ungodly: right to ask God's mind, but perilously placed to hear it, where the counsel most pleasing is least likely to be true.
5:
Ahab answers the call for God's word by assembling a chorus of four hundred, and the witnesses read their unanimous "Go up" as the very picture of flattery masquerading as prophecy. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott attends to the wording. These are "the prophets" with the article, the king's own establishment; where the older text at 1 Kings 22:6 has "about four hundred," the chronicler rounds the number, and in their answer he writes Adonai, "the Lord," rather than ha-elohim, "the true God" — a change that quietly withholds the covenant name from the mouths of these court-prophets. Ellicott notes too that the chronicler has Ahab ask "shall I go" where Kings has "shall we go," and reads "I go against" for the parallel's "we go to" — the king speaking throughout as the one sovereign who leads the war, the four hundred merely ratifying what he has already resolved. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sums the scene from his survey of the chapter: they consult the prophets concerning the success of the war, and all, except Micaiah, promise Ahab victory.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry fastens on the unhappiness of a man surrounded by such voices. Here is the misery of those hemmed in by flatterers, and especially by flattering prophets, who cry peace and prophesy nothing but smooth things. Thus, Henry says, was Ahab cheated into his ruin, and justly; for he hearkened to such men and preferred those who humoured him before a faithful prophet who would give him fair warning of his danger. Those do best for themselves who give their friends, and particularly their ministers, leave to deal plainly and faithfully with them, and take reproof not only patiently but kindly — "for that counsel is not always best for us that is most pleasing to us."

The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott exposes the careful diction by which the chronicler marks these four hundred as less than true prophets of Jehovah; Clarke sets their chorus over against the one dissenting voice to come; Henry reads the whole muster as the tragedy of a king who assembled prophets not to learn God's will but to have his own confirmed. The unanimity that should have reassured Ahab is the surest sign the word is false, for four hundred voices agreeing to please a king are no substitute for one that will tell him the truth. The very number of them is meant to impress, yet a lie does not become truth by being multiplied, nor does a prophet become God's by drawing his bread from the king's table. It is against this smooth and crowded chorus that Jehoshaphat, uneasy, will ask whether there is not yet a prophet of the LORD besides.
6:
Unsatisfied with the confident chorus, Jehoshaphat presses further — "Is there not here a prophet of the LORD besides, that we might inquire of him?" — and the witnesses find in that single word "besides" a quiet verdict on the four hundred. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes only the connective, that the chronicler opens with "and" where the common version reads "but," the phrase standing exactly as the literal Hebrew of 1 Kings 22:7. The smallness of the note belies the weight of the question, for by asking for a prophet of the LORD "besides" these, Jehoshaphat tacitly disowns the whole assembly Ahab had gathered: whatever they were — court-prophets, or servants of the calves the northern kingdom had set up — they were not, to his ear, prophets of Jehovah whose word could be trusted. It took no small courage to say so, standing in another king's palace before a confident host of four hundred; but the pious king would rather risk the awkwardness than march on an assurance he did not believe.

Here the discernment the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry had marked in the good king shows itself. Jehoshaphat, for all his fault in keeping such company, could not rest in the smooth assurances of men who cried peace; something in him wanted the fair warning of a true prophet rather than the humouring of false ones, and so he would not march on the strength of four hundred voices until he had heard whether one voice of the LORD might yet be found. It is the same instinct that had made him call for inquiry at the word of the LORD in the verse before — an instinct sound in itself, though strangely lodged in a man who had put himself in a place where such inquiry was so unwelcome.

The witnesses leave the verse where the narrative leaves it, poised on a pointed question. Ellicott secures the text and its connective; the sense the passage yields, and which Henry's reading confirms, is that Jehoshaphat's request is the hinge on which the whole scene turns. Ahab's crowded court has spoken with one mouth, and the king of Judah is not persuaded. The demand for a prophet "besides" forces into the open the one man Ahab has kept back — the man he hates because he never prophesies good — and so opens the door to the true word that the four hundred had drowned out. A good man's holy dissatisfaction with easy answers becomes, under God, the means by which the truth is at last let in.
7:
Ahab's reply lays his heart bare — "There is yet one man... but I hate him; for he never prophesied good unto me, but always evil" — and the witnesses probe both the king's hatred and Jehoshaphat's gentle rebuke. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott observes that the chronicler has aggravated the note of opposition: where Kings has simply "he prophesieth not good but evil," here it is "he is not prophesying to me for good, but all his days for evil" — that is, throughout the whole course of his prophetic career. The prophet's name he traces with care: Micaiah, Hebrew Mikayehu, means "Who is like Iah?" — Iah being in all likelihood the oldest form of the divine Name; and "Imla," his father's name, means "he is full" or "he filleth," etymologically right. The closing words, "Let not the king say so," Ellicott reads as Jehoshaphat hearing in Ahab's complaint a presentiment of evil and deprecating the omen — as though the king of Judah shrank from a saying that seemed to forebode the very disaster to come.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the reproof and finds it too faint. Jehoshaphat, he says, could scarcely find in his heart to give Ahab even a mild and gentle rebuke for hating a prophet of the LORD; a bolder friend would have pressed the point home. Ahab's very complaint against Micaiah — that he never prophesies good — is in truth his highest commendation, for a prophet's business is not to flatter but to tell the truth, and a king who hates a man for always telling him the truth has condemned himself. Yet Jehoshaphat, entangled in the courtesies of his host, ventures no more than "Let not the king say so," and lets the matter drop.

The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott unfolds the language — the heightened "all his days," the name that asks "Who is like Jah?", the deprecated omen; Henry measures the moral temperature of the scene, where a good king's rebuke of a wicked one's malice toward God's prophet is softened almost to nothing by the awkwardness of the table he sits at. Between them they show the true prophet named at last, hated by the king who needs him most, and defended by the king who should defend him better — the whole exchange turning on the terrible fact that Ahab measured a prophet's worth by whether his words were pleasant, and hated the one man in his realm who would not lie to him.
8:
The order to fetch Micaiah is given in a single hurried line, and the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott alone attends to it, chiefly through its words. "Called for one of his officers," he notes, is literally "called to a eunuch" — one of the class of court-servants such as those set over the royal household, comparable to the officials named at 1 Chronicles 28:1; and the prophet's name here appears in the contracted Hebrew form Mikahu, for which the margin substitutes the usual spelling. Small as these observations are, they let us see the machinery of the court in motion: a king who keeps his officers at hand and dispatches one at once, so that the man he hates may be brought with all speed to the gate where the two kings sit enthroned.

The verse repays the reader who marks its place in the drama. Ahab has been forced, by Jehoshaphat's insistence, to send for the very prophet he would rather have forgotten; and he does so without delay, calling to the eunuch "Fetch quickly Micaiah the son of Imla." There is a grim irony in the promptness. The king who has surrounded himself with four hundred agreeable voices, and who confessed a moment before that he hated the one man who told him the truth, must now summon that man in haste before a watching ally — and the summoning is the beginning of his undoing, for the word he does not wish to hear is already on its way. The eunuch dispatched at the king's word becomes, all unknowing, the servant of a higher summons; the officer sent to fetch a prophet is fetching the sentence of heaven.

Ellicott's philological care, which might seem to touch only the surface of the text, in fact steadies the ground under the story: this is history, told with the exactness of a chronicler who knows the titles of the court and the true form of a prophet's name. The eunuch goes; Micaiah is fetched; and the stage is set, between the enthroned kings and the clamouring prophets, for the entrance of the solitary man of God whose single sentence will outweigh the four hundred. The bare notice of a servant sent on an errand is, in the economy of the narrative, the hinge that swings open the scene of judgment to come, and prepares the reader to weigh one true word against the whole chorus of false ones.
9:
The scene is set with almost theatrical care — the two kings enthroned in their robes at the gate of Samaria, and the prophets raving before them — and the witnesses attend both to the staging and to the contrast of the two kings' hearts. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke gives the Targum's pointed gloss: Ahab consulted false prophets, but Jehoshaphat sought instruction from the presence of the LORD and prayed at the entering in of Samaria; and before these two the false prophets prophesied lies. The paraphrase draws the moral the scene itself implies — that at the same gate one king leaned on flattery and the other on prayer.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott brings his usual precision to the picture. "Sat either of them on his throne" he would render "were sitting each on his throne"; and the clause "clothed in their robes" he marks as difficult, for the pronoun that the sense requires is wanting in the Hebrew, and the Syriac may preserve an older reading, "clothed in raiment spotted white and black." The "void place" where the thrones stood he takes to be a threshing-floor — the open ground of the Septuagint, the level place of the Vulgate — though he suspects the word itself corrupt, perhaps arising out of beruddim, "spotted" or embroidered, an epithet of the royal robes. "Prophesied," he adds, is properly "were prophesying," the whole company in full cry as the kings looked on; the Septuagint sets the thrones "in the open ground," the Vulgate in a threshing-floor, and the very uncertainty of the versions shows how difficult the word had already become to those who first rendered it.

The witnesses do not divide. Clarke, through the Targum, reads the theology of the tableau — two kings, two trusts, one seeking God and one seeking his own reassurance; Ellicott recovers the exact staging and the vexed words that describe it. Between them they let the verse do its work as the frame of the great confrontation: the pomp of the enthroned monarchs in their bright apparel, the din of four hundred prophets promising victory, and, unspoken but felt, the emptiness at the heart of it all. It is a scene of splendid outward assurance into which one solitary contrary voice is about to be led, and the very magnificence of the setting — thrones, robes, and a shouting chorus — only sharpens the coming clash between the crowd that pleases and the prophet who does not.
10:
One of the four hundred now steps beyond words into acted prophecy: Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah makes himself horns of iron and cries, "With these shalt thou push Syria until they be consumed." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes the force of the image. The verb "push" is properly "butt," the action of a horned beast goring its foe, the same word used of the ram butting westward and northward in Daniel's vision at Daniel 8:4, and applied figuratively to the tribes of Joseph pushing the peoples to the ends of the earth at Deuteronomy 33:17. The closing phrase, "until they be consumed," he renders "unto destroying them" — a promise of total victory, nothing left of the Syrian host, the annihilation absolute and unqualified.

The iron horns are a bold counterfeit of the true prophets' sign-acts, borrowing the very language of blessing that Moses had pronounced on Joseph's warlike strength. Zedekiah, ringleader of the flattering chorus, does not merely echo the others' "Go up and prosper"; he dramatizes it, thrusting the imagined horns before the enthroned kings as though the conquest were already visible. The gesture lends his lie the outward form of inspiration, and it is precisely this confidence — a prophet who acts as well as speaks — that makes the deception so nearly irresistible. And the text is careful to add that he did not act alone: all the prophets prophesied so, the iron horns of the one becoming the emblem of the whole chorus. The horns that promise to gore Syria to destruction are wielded by a man who will presently strike the true prophet of the LORD across the face.

Ellicott's philological care keeps the reader's feet on the ground of the text, but it also opens the verse's deeper irony. The word "consumed" foretells a destruction that will indeed come at Ramoth-gilead — not to Syria, but to the king who trusts the iron horns. Zedekiah promises Ahab that he shall push his enemies to their ruin; the arrow drawn "at a venture" will push Ahab to his. The verse stands as the high-water mark of the false prophets' assurance, the whole company gathered behind a dramatic pledge of victory that the God who permits the lie has already turned into a snare. What is staged as the triumph of Israel is, in the secret purpose of heaven, the baiting of a doomed king.
11:
The chorus swells to unanimity — "all the prophets prophesied so, saying, Go up to Ramoth-gilead, and prosper" — and the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott makes the very word "prophesied" open a window on what prophecy was meant to be. Here the participle is nibbe'im, "were prophesying," while at v.9 the synonym used, mithnabbe'im, carries the further sense of "raving" or acting the madman, as of the ecstatic in Jeremiah 29:26. The root, he explains, is likely visible in the Assyrian nabu, "to call, proclaim," so that the nabi, the prophet, is properly the spokesman of God, the herald of heaven to earth — the same idea preserved in the name of the Babylonian god Nebo. "And prosper" he reads as a confident "thou shalt prosper," an imperative of promise like "This do, and live," or the assurance given Abimelech at Genesis 20:7, "he shall pray for thee, and live thou" — the grammar itself pressing the certainty of a victory that would never come. The god Nebo, whose name embodies the same root, was reckoned among the heathen the very scribe and herald of the gods; how much more, then, ought a herald of the living God to carry only what he was given to carry.

The irony Ellicott's philology exposes is exact. These men bear the honourable name of heralds of heaven, spokesmen of God, and every one of them speaks a lie; the whole company, four hundred strong, proclaims with one mouth a word God never gave. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke had marked the point in his survey of the chapter — all, save Micaiah, promise Ahab victory — and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry the tragedy behind it, that a king cheated by such smooth unanimity was cheated to his ruin, having preferred those who humoured him to the one who would have warned him.

The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott recovers the dignity of the word these men profaned; Clarke and Henry press the moral weight of their agreement. The perfect concord of the four hundred, which to Ahab was proof enough, is to the reader the surest mark of falsehood: heralds who all cry "prosper" to please their king have forgotten that a herald's office is to carry his master's word and not his hearer's wish. The one true herald of heaven is still outside the gate, and his word, when it comes, will stand alone against them all — a single spokesman of God against four hundred spokesmen of a lie.
12:
The messenger sent to fetch Micaiah tries to school him on the way, urging him to make his word agree with the rest — "the words of the prophets declare good to the king with one assent; let thy word therefore, I pray thee, be like one of theirs." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott attends to the phrasing. "With one assent" is literally "one mouth," the same idiom that describes the Canaanite kings gathering "with one accord" to fight Israel at Joshua 9:2; and instead of "the words of the prophets," he suggests, we should probably read "the prophets have with one mouth spoken good" — a far slighter change in the Hebrew than in English. The closing plea, "like one of theirs," he compares with the fuller form of Kings, "like the word of one of them" — the officer reducing the whole question of God's will to a matter of falling in with the majority.

The verse lays bare the pressure brought to bear on a faithful man. The officer does not threaten; he cajoles, appealing to the comfort of numbers and the safety of agreement — four hundred voices have said one thing, and it will go easier with the prophet, and with the king's temper, if his makes four hundred and one. It is the ancient temptation of the true minister to trim his message to the consensus around him, to speak smooth things because smooth things are expected, and to let the majority settle what only God may settle. The messenger's counsel is worldly wisdom itself: why stand alone, and why provoke a king, when a single agreeable word would buy peace? He assumes, as the world always assumes, that four hundred cannot be wrong and one cannot be right — that truth is settled by a show of hands rather than by the voice of God.

Ellicott's care with the "one mouth" of the prophets sharpens the contrast the next verse will draw. The whole apparatus of the scene — the crowd, the unanimity, the friendly warning — is arranged to bend Micaiah to the chorus. But the prophet who is about to answer has taken his stand on other ground: not on what the prophets have spoken with one mouth, but on what the LORD will put in his. The verse thus prepares the reader for the great refusal, setting the full weight of consensus and self-interest against the solitary conscience that will not be moved, and letting us feel how much it costs to speak the one word that all the world has agreed shall not be spoken.
13:
Micaiah's answer to the messenger is an oath of unbending fidelity — "As the LORD liveth, even what my God saith, that will I speak" — and the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens both its force and its wording. The word rendered "even" he would give as "nay, but": not a mild addition to the messenger's plea but a flat refusal of it — "nay, but whatsoever my God shall say, that will I speak." And where the older text at 1 Kings 22:14 reads "whatsoever the LORD saith," the chronicler writes "my God" — the possessive laying claim, in the prophet's mouth, to a personal allegiance the four hundred had forfeited. The one small pronoun marks the whole difference between a hireling and a servant: the court-prophets spoke the king's word for the king's bread, but Micaiah owns a God who is his, and to that God alone he will answer.

The oath answers, point for point, the pressure of the verse before. The messenger had asked him to make his word "like one of theirs"; Micaiah swears it shall be like none of theirs, but only like the word of God. He binds himself with the most solemn form Israel knew, "as the LORD liveth," and stakes everything on a single principle: that a prophet is not the servant of the consensus, nor of the king, nor of his own safety, but only of the word given him. Whatever God shall say — whether smooth or bitter, whether it please the king or cost the prophet his liberty — that, and that alone, will he speak. It is the charter of every true minister of the word, that he is bound not to gratify his hearers but to deliver his message, and that faithfulness, not acceptability, is the measure of his office.

Ellicott's small corrections carry the whole weight of the man's integrity. The "nay, but" marks the refusal; the "my God" marks the loyalty. Here is the true herald of heaven the earlier verses had defined by contrast: where the four hundred spoke to please and the messenger counselled him to conform, Micaiah will speak to be faithful, though he stand alone against them all. The verse is the still centre of the chapter's storm — one man's quiet vow, sworn by the living God, that no crowd and no crown shall put a word in his mouth that God has not put there first. It is on the strength of this oath that everything which follows, the mockery, the blow, the prison, and the vindication, will unfold.
14:
Brought at last before the kings, Micaiah answers Ahab's question with words that echo the four hundred so exactly that they can only be irony — "Go up, and prosper, and they shall be delivered into your hand." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes first the small variation in the king's question, "shall I forbear" where Kings has "shall we forbear," and then the more telling change in the answer. Where the older text simply repeats Zedekiah's promise of v.11, the chronicler gives a reply that states quite definitely that they — the Syrians — shall be delivered up, an object the earlier promise had left unexpressed. The effect, Ellicott remarks, is like the ambiguity of the Delphic oracle that told Croesus if he crossed the Halys he would overthrow a mighty empire — his own, as it proved — though Micaiah's mockery is transparent enough to any ear willing to hear it.

The prophet's meaning lies not in the words but in the way of them. He has been adjured to speak, watched by two kings and jeered at by four hundred; and so he throws the flatterers' own phrase back at them, "Go up and prosper," in a tone so plainly hollow that Ahab himself, as the next verse shows, cannot mistake it. It is holy sarcasm — the truth spoken in the very language of the lie, so that the king who wished to be humoured is humoured to his face and feels the sting of it. Micaiah will not yet give the true oracle; he first holds up to Ahab the emptiness of the assurance the king has been feeding on. There is a stern mercy in the method, for by mimicking the flatterers the prophet gives Ahab one last chance to hear how hollow their chorus rings, and to ask, if he dares, for something better than an echo.

Ellicott's comparison with the double-tongued oracle of Delphi is apt but limited, for he is careful to add that Zedekiah's words, and Micaiah's echo of them, were plain enough. There is no real ambiguity here, only irony: the phrase that promised victory is turned into a mirror in which Ahab may see the folly of trusting it. The verse thus marks the turn of the whole scene. The prophet who swore he would speak only what God said has begun to speak — and his first word is a deliberate, cutting repetition of the lie, offered so that the king may be forced to demand the truth he has been at such pains to avoid.
15:
Ahab, stung by the irony, drops his own pretence and demands the truth — "How many times shall I adjure thee that thou say nothing but the truth to me in the name of the LORD?" The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes that the verse stands word for word as 1 Kings 22:16, and draws one arresting comparison for the act of adjuring: it is the same solemn charge the high priest laid upon Christ before the council, "I adjure thee by the living God, that thou tell us whether thou be the Christ," at Matthew 26:63. The parallel is heavy with meaning. In both scenes a hostile authority binds a truthful witness by the name of God to speak, and in both the truth, once spoken, seals the speaker's condemnation.

The moment is thick with self-contradiction. Ahab has assembled four hundred prophets precisely to avoid the truth, has confessed that he hates Micaiah for never prophesying good, and has just been mocked with his own flatterers' words; now he suddenly stands upon the honour of the divine Name and demands sincerity, as though he had wanted it all along. The king who would not hear the truth when it was hidden cannot bear it when it is disguised as flattery, and so he adjures the prophet to strip off the irony. It is the strange compulsion of conscience even in a hardened man: Ahab must know, though knowing will not turn him. The very solemnity of the oath he demands — "in the name of the LORD" — condemns the four hundred at a stroke, for it confesses that their smooth chorus was not spoken in that Name at all, and that the king had always known the difference between a flatterer and a prophet.

Ellicott's single comparison opens the verse toward its darkest depth. Micaiah, adjured by the name of the LORD to speak nothing but truth, is in the place where every faithful witness of God has stood — the place where Christ himself would stand before Caiaphas — charged on oath to tell a truth that his hearers have already resolved to punish. The adjuration is not a genuine seeking of guidance but a demand that the prophet commit himself, so that his testimony may be used against him. And Micaiah, like his Lord after him, will answer the charge fully, knowing that the truth he is about to utter will earn him not a hearing but a prison. The verse turns the king's impatience into the occasion of the true oracle at last.
16:
Now Micaiah speaks the true word, and it is a vision of desolation — "I saw all Israel scattered upon the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott marks the small differences from the older text: "upon the mountains" where Kings has "unto the mountains," and "as sheep" more fully rendered "like the flock," a flock of both sheep and goats driven leaderless over the hills. The image is unmistakable in its import. A scattered flock without a shepherd is an army without its king; and to say that Israel is so scattered is to foretell, plainly now and without irony, that the king who leads them up to Ramoth-gilead will not lead them home.

Micaiah's oracle answers the adjuration exactly. Charged to speak nothing but the truth in the name of the LORD, he gives not the promised victory of the four hundred but a picture of defeat and a masterless people; and he adds the LORD's own word upon it, "These have no master; let them return every man to his house in peace" — a bitter peace, the peace of a war given up because its leader is dead. The figure of the shepherdless sheep is one Scripture uses for a people bereft of guidance and exposed to every danger — the very fear that moved Moses to pray for a successor lest the congregation be "as sheep which have no shepherd" at Numbers 27:17, and the compassion that moved the Lord Jesus over the fainting multitudes at Matthew 9:36. Here it falls upon Ahab like a sentence: the shepherd shall be struck, and the flock scattered.

Ellicott's quiet notes on the prepositions do not blunt the force of the vision; they only fix its wording as the chronicler preserved it. What the verse gives is the exact reversal of everything the crowded court had promised. The prophets cried "prosper"; Micaiah sees rout. They dramatized conquest with horns of iron; he sees a leaderless flock straggling home. And the tragedy is that the true word, once given, changes nothing in the king who demanded it — Ahab will hear his own death foretold in the image of the shepherdless sheep and march out to fulfil it. The vision of scattered Israel stands as the heart of the chapter's warning: that the God who is mocked by four hundred flatterers will yet make one prophet's word come true upon the mountains of Gilead.
17:
Ahab turns to his guest with a note of sour vindication — "Did I not tell thee that he would not prophesy good unto me, but evil?" The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott observes only that the phrase "but evil" stands as in Kings, with a slight variation the Hebrew margin corrects, and refers the reader back to the king's earlier complaint at v.7, where Ahab had first named his grievance against the prophet. The repetition is the point: the king has heard the true oracle, and his response is not fear, nor repentance, nor even argument, but a peevish "I told you so," as if the prophet's faithfulness were merely a personal spite against himself.

Here the whole tragedy of Ahab is laid bare in a sentence. He has just been told that his army will be scattered like sheep without a shepherd, and he hears in it nothing but confirmation of his long complaint that Micaiah never says anything pleasant. He measures the word of God entirely by its agreeableness to himself; a prophecy of defeat can only mean that the prophet is against him, never that God is warning him. The truth that should have stopped him in his tracks he treats as a grudge to be resented, turning to Jehoshaphat almost in triumph, as though the very darkness of the message proved Micaiah unworthy of belief. It is a strange logic, but a common one: to argue that because a warning is unwelcome it must be untrue, and to take the faithfulness of the warner as the surest proof of his malice. Ahab has heard the counsel of heaven declared to his face, and he can find nothing in it but an old personal quarrel — the message swallowed up, in his hearing, by his hatred of the messenger.

Ellicott's cross-reference to v.7 quietly frames the man. What Ahab said before he heard the oracle he says again after: his mind was made up, and no vision of scattered Israel could unmake it. The verse shows a heart so set on its own course that the plainest warning becomes only fresh evidence of the warner's ill-will. And in that refusal to hear lies the whole justice of what follows, for a king who will construe the truth of God as personal malice has already chosen his end. Ahab's "Did I not tell thee?" is the epitaph of every man who hates the messenger because he cannot bear the message.
18:
Micaiah presses on to the ground of his oracle, opening the veil on a heavenly council — "Hear the word of the LORD: I saw the LORD sitting upon his throne, and all the host of heaven standing on his right hand and on his left." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes the chronicler's connectives and abridgements: "and" for "again," the prophet's "hear ye" where Kings has "hear thou," and the shortening of the older description, "all the host of heaven standing by him, on his right hand and on his left." The Vulgate, he adds, renders the sense excellently — "but he said, Therefore hear the word of the LORD." The vision is set over against the whole preceding scene: two earthly kings sat on their thrones in their robes, and four hundred prophets stood before them; now the prophet lifts the curtain and shows the true throne, and the true court, before which the courts of Samaria are a shadow.

The theology of the picture is its power. Micaiah does not merely contradict the four hundred; he explains them. Above the enthroned kings of earth sits the enthroned LORD of heaven, attended by the whole angelic host as a monarch by his councillors; and it is from that council, as the following verses will show, that the fate of Ahab has been determined. The prophet claims to have stood where no false prophet ever stood — in the deliberations of God — and to report not a guess about the battle but a decree already passed in the court above. The vision answers, at a stroke, the question of authority: whose word shall the kings trust, the four hundred who flatter, or the one who has seen the throne?

Ellicott's attention to the chronicler's compression keeps the reader aware that this is a faithful, if briefer, transcript of the older record. But the abridgement takes nothing from the majesty of the scene. Micaiah sets the shepherdless flock of his first vision within a larger frame: Israel scattered on the mountains because a sentence has been handed down in heaven. The verse turns the whole confrontation from a dispute between prophets into a disclosure of the divine government, in which even the lie that will lure Ahab to his death is shown to proceed, by permission, from the throne the prophet has seen. It is the boldest claim a man of God can make — that he has heard the counsel of the Almighty — and on its truth the rest of the chapter depends.
19:
The vision unfolds into a startling scene of heavenly deliberation — "And the LORD said, Who shall entice Ahab king of Israel, that he may go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead? And one spake saying after this manner, and another saying after that manner." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms the text against those who would smooth it, rendering the picture of the council literally: "and one said thus, and another said thus" — the members of the heavenly host offering, each in turn, his own counsel, as courtiers debating before a king. The variation in the Hebrew word for "after this manner," where Kings has a slightly different form, he judges a mere matter of spelling; the sense, he insists, is certainly right.

The boldness of the vision has troubled many, and rightly repays care. The LORD is represented as asking who will entice Ahab to his fall, and the spirits of the council proposing this way and that, until one comes forward with a plan that is approved. It is a scene framed in the language of a royal court — much like the council in which the sons of God present themselves before the LORD at Job 1:6 — precisely so that a truth beyond human sight may be made plain: that Ahab's ruin is no accident of battle but the execution of a sentence, and that the very deception which will draw him out is not outside God's government but proposed and permitted within it. The plurality of voices — one saying thus, another thus — marks the reality of the deliberation, the decree taking shape as the counsel is weighed.

Ellicott's defence of the text against emendation matters here, for the temptation has always been to soften a passage that shows a lying spirit taking its commission before the throne of God. But the chronicler, faithfully following the older record, will not have it softened, and the prophet reports what he saw. The question "Who shall entice Ahab?" is the hinge of the whole vision: it reveals that the king's death is willed in heaven, that the means of it will be a deception, and that the four hundred prophets whose unanimous word Ahab has trusted are the instruments of that very enticement. What the next verses name, this verse sets in motion — the fatal counsel that will send a doomed king up to Ramoth-gilead persuaded that he goes to victory.
20:
The counsel of heaven comes to a point: "Then there came out a spirit, and stood before the LORD, and said, I will entice him." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott would render the opening more exactly, "And the spirit came forth" — with the article, as if a particular spirit now steps out of the host to take the commission the LORD had invited. The definiteness is not idle; it marks the moment the vague deliberation of the council resolves into a single volunteer, one spirit undertaking the work of enticement that will draw Ahab to Ramoth-gilead. Where the many had proposed this way and that, one now steps forward with a plan, and the Septuagint's plain "and the spirit came forth" fixes the turn from debate to decision.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke records the strange gloss the Targum fastens upon the scene, which names the spirit that came forth as the spirit of Naboth of Jezreel, come out from the abode of the righteous to stand before the LORD and offer to be a spirit of false prophecy in the mouth of Ahab's prophets. The LORD, in the paraphrase, grants the power but bars the spirit from returning to sit among the righteous, since no one who speaks falsely may keep a mansion there, and sends it forth to do as it had said. Clarke reports the tradition as a curiosity, the rabbis reaching for a reason why judicial deception should light on Ahab of all men — the blood of the murdered innocent crying still for vengeance.

The witnesses do not divide over the substance. Ellicott fixes the grammar that singles out the volunteer spirit; Clarke preserves the Jewish fancy that would give it a name and a motive. Between them they hold the reader before the hard mystery of the verse: that a spirit of falsehood presents itself in the divine council, offers its service, and is commissioned there. The chronicler does not flinch from it, and neither may his interpreters. Whatever the Targum's embroidery, the plain sense stands — that the enticement which will ruin Ahab was proposed before the throne of God and permitted to go forward, so that the king's own trusted prophets became, by heaven's sufferance, the very engine of his fall. The vision does not make God the author of the lie, but it does declare that no lie, and no liar, moves beyond the reach of his government.
21:
The spirit names its method — "I will go out, and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets" — and the LORD's answer seals the commission: "Thou shalt entice him, and prevail also: go out, and do so." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes that the phrase is literally "I will become a spirit of falsehood," and gathers the sober parallels that keep the verse from being softened away. Scripture elsewhere speaks of a spirit poured out for confusion, as upon Egypt at Isaiah 19:14, and most solemnly of the LORD himself deceiving a self-willed prophet at Ezekiel 14:9 — "if the prophet be deceived when he hath spoken a thing, I the LORD have deceived that prophet." The verb rendered "entice," he adds, is pittah, the same word used throughout the vision, which the Septuagint gives as "thou shalt deceive"; and he points to the New Testament's own version of the principle, the strong delusion God sends upon those who receive not the love of the truth, at 2 Thessalonians 2:11.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the two doctrines the verse presses upon the conscience. First, the power of Satan, by the divine permission, in the children of disobedience: one lying spirit can make four hundred lying prophets, and use them to deceive Ahab, for the devil becomes a murderer by being a liar and destroys men by deceiving them. Second, the justice of God in giving up to strong delusions, to believe a lie, those who will not receive the love of the truth but rebel against it: let the lying spirit prevail to entice those to their ruin who would not be persuaded to their duty and their happiness. The deception, in Henry's reading, is at once Satan's work and God's righteous sentence — the liar doing his own will, and by that very act executing the judgment of heaven upon a king who loved to be deceived.

The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott ranges the Scriptures that show God overruling and even sending deception as judgment; Henry weighs the moral justice of it. Between them they guard the verse's hardest truth without blunting it: that God is not the author of falsehood, yet he governs it, so that the very lie Ahab preferred becomes the instrument of the doom he had earned. The spirit goes out to fill four hundred mouths; and the God who permits it does so because a man who will not hear the truth has forfeited his right to be kept from the lie. The commission "go out, and do so" is not the corruption of heaven's justice but its terrible fulfilment.
22:
Micaiah draws the vision to its point-blank application — "Now therefore, behold, the LORD hath put a lying spirit in the mouth of these thy prophets, and the LORD hath spoken evil against thee." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes the chronicler's wording, "and now" for "now therefore," and "these thy prophets" where Kings and several manuscripts read "all these," the fuller phrase sweeping in the whole four hundred. The prophet does not leave the heavenly vision hanging as a marvel; he brings it down upon Ahab's head with the word "therefore." The council he saw, the volunteer spirit, the commission granted — all of it means one thing for the king before him: the prophets he has trusted are the mouthpieces of the very deception decreed against him, and the God whose favour they promised has in truth spoken his ruin.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley fastens on the same lesson the puritan witness had drawn from the verse before: "See the power of Satan! One lying spirit can make four hundred lying prophets. And thus he frequently becomes a murderer by being a liar, and destroys men by deceiving them." The horror of the thing is its economy — a single spirit of falsehood, going out from the council of God, is enough to turn a whole college of prophets into instruments of death, and to lead a king smiling to his grave. The lie is the murderer's weapon; deception does what the sword cannot, disarming the victim of all suspicion until the trap is sprung. And the deepest terror of Wesley's word is that the same Satan who fills the false prophets' mouths does his work by the divine permission, so that even his triumph serves the justice he means to defy.

The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott fixes the compass of "these thy prophets"; Wesley presses the power of the deceiver behind them. Between them they let Micaiah's "therefore" fall with full weight. The prophet has done all that a faithful man can do: he has told the king plainly that his counsellors are lying, that the lie is permitted by God as judgment, and that the word gone forth against him is evil and not good. Nothing is hidden; the whole machinery of the deception is exposed to Ahab's face before ever he marches. And this is the terror of the verse — that a man may be warned of the very lie he believes, be shown its source and its end, and still choose it. Micaiah has unmasked the four hundred; it remains to be seen whether Ahab will heed the one.
23:
The truth, spoken plainly, is answered with a blow — Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah, ringleader of the four hundred, strikes Micaiah on the cheek and sneers, "Which way went the Spirit of the LORD from me to speak unto thee?" The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes the chronicler's characteristic touch in the verb "smote," a shortened form of the fuller word in Kings, one of the small corrections he often makes; and he renders the taunt literally, "where is the way the Spirit of Jehovah passed to speak with thee?" The false prophet, the maker of the iron horns, cannot bear to be publicly branded a liar, and answers argument with violence and violence with mockery.

The question is meant as ridicule but is in truth an unwitting confession. Zedekiah does not deny that the Spirit of the LORD spoke through him; he demands to know by what road that Spirit could have left him to reach Micaiah — as if inspiration were his possession and no true word could come but through his mouth. It is the arrogance of the established majority affronted by a lone dissenter: the four hundred are the recognized prophets, the court is on their side, and the notion that the Spirit should pass them by and speak through the one man they despise is, to Zedekiah, an absurdity worth a blow. Yet his very words concede the ground, for they ask not whether but by what way the Spirit went — and the answer, as the next verse gives it, is that Zedekiah will learn the way soon enough, when he flees to hide himself.

Ellicott's small notes on the verbs keep the scene exact, but the verse needs little gloss to strike home. It is the ancient lot of the faithful witness, that the truth earns him not a hearing but a hand across the face; the prophet who has just laid bare the counsel of heaven is treated as a madman and an impostor by the man whose lie he exposed. The blow of Zedekiah is the world's standing answer to the word it will not receive, and Micaiah bears it in silence, as the prelude to the prison that waits — the true prophet struck across the face for telling the truth, in a scene that later ages would see repeated when a greater than Micaiah stood bound before his accusers and was smitten for his witness. The Spirit of the LORD did indeed pass by the four hundred to speak through the one; and the striker who mocks that truth will live to see it proved upon himself.
24:
Micaiah answers the blow not with a blow but with a prophecy of Zedekiah's shame — "Behold, thou shalt see on that day when thou shalt go into an inner chamber to hide thyself." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the opening "thou art to see," or "destined to see," and the hiding-place literally as "a chamber within a chamber," the innermost room of a house, where the false prophet will one day cower. He observes too, with Ewald, that Zedekiah's further history is nowhere recorded — an indication that the original narrative from which this account is drawn contained much more than the present extract, and that the day of his hiding was once told at length in a fuller record now lost.

The prophecy is exactly fitted to the taunt. Zedekiah had demanded to know which way the Spirit of the LORD had gone; Micaiah replies that he shall know on the day of reckoning, when the defeat he denied has come to pass and he flees from room to room to hide from the vengeance of a people undeceived. The man who struck the true prophet in the confidence of the court will learn the truth in terror and concealment, no longer the honoured spokesman of a king but a hunted liar seeking the deepest chamber. It is the standing pattern of false prophecy: bold in the day of flattery, and cowering in the day when the word it despised is fulfilled. The chamber within a chamber, where no flatterer's fee can follow him and no crowd of fellow-prophets can shield him, is the true wage of a lie told in God's name.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the verse into his reflection on the whole scene, that the persecutors of God's faithful ministers will be "made to see in that day" what they will not now believe. The day always comes that declares who was in the right and who in the wrong; and Zedekiah's hidden chamber is the emblem of every scoffer's reckoning, when the truth he mocked overtakes him and the flattery he traded in leaves him no shelter. Ellicott's note that the sequel is lost only sharpens the point: Scripture keeps the prophecy and lets the fulfilment be assumed, so that the verse stands as warning rather than record — the sentence pronounced, the fugitive's terror foretold, and the reader left to know that the word of the LORD does not fall to the ground, though the false prophet strike the true one across the face.
25:
Ahab's response to the true prophecy is not repentance but arrest — "Take ye Micaiah, and carry him back to Amon the governor of the city, and to Joash the king's son." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes that the chronicler has the king address several attendants, "take ye... carry him," where Kings speaks to a single officer, "take thou... carry thou"; the "governor" he glosses as sar, a prefect or ruler of the city, the officer set over Samaria; and "carry back" he takes to mean convey him back, literally "make him return" — for the prophet is to be returned to custody, sent back to the keeping he had presumably been fetched from.

The order is chillingly matter-of-fact. Ahab does not argue with the vision of scattered Israel, nor answer the charge that his prophets are liars and God has spoken evil against him; he simply removes the man who spoke it. To hand Micaiah over to the governor and to the king's son is to file him away as a nuisance, to be dealt with by the ordinary machinery of the state. There is no attempt to disprove the prophecy, because Ahab does not mean to weigh it; he means to silence it and march. The very calm of the command is its condemnation, the act of a man who has heard his death foretold and answers by jailing the messenger. That the prophet is committed to "the governor of the city" and to "the king's son" shows how ordinary the business is made to seem — a matter for the civil authorities, a name entered on a warrant — as though the counsel of heaven could be filed away with the other affairs of state.

Ellicott's small philological notes — the plural attendants, the prefect's title, the sense of "make him return" — keep the administrative reality of the scene in view. This is how kingdoms have always dealt with inconvenient truth: not by refuting it but by processing its bearer, delivering him to an officer and a warrant. Micaiah, who has stood in the council of heaven and reported its decree, is consigned to Amon and to Joash as though he were a common offender. The verse marks the world's verdict on the word of God — that a prophecy of doom is a breach of public order — and prepares the reader for the sentence of bread and water that Ahab is about to pronounce, the petty cruelty of a doomed king toward the one man who told him the truth.
26:
The sentence upon the prophet is bread and water and a prison — "Put this fellow in the prison, and feed him with bread of affliction and with water of affliction, until I return in peace." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the phrase "of affliction": the word lahats is not a genitive but an accusative, so that the sense is "bread with stint" and "water with stint" — bread and water measured out sparingly, literally "squeezing," as the Vulgate renders it, "a little bread and a little water." He compares the scanty fare of adversity in Isaiah 30:20, "the bread of adversity and the water of affliction"; and he notes that the chronicler's "until I return in peace" is a correction of the older "until I come."

The words "until I return in peace" are Ahab's last defiance of the prophecy, and they recoil upon him. He has just been told that the flock of Israel shall be scattered for want of a shepherd; he answers by ordering the prophet kept on prison rations until he comes home victorious — staking, as it were, Micaiah's release on his own survival. It is bravado in the teeth of the word of God, and Micaiah will seize on it at once. The starving of the prophet is the meanness of a king who cannot refute the truth and so revenges himself upon the truth-teller, doling out affliction by the mouthful to the man who would not flatter him.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads in the contemptuous "this fellow" the long history of the faithful minister's lot: "How frequently has this been the lot of faithful ministers, to be hated and ill treated, merely for being true to God, and just and kind to the souls of men!" But the wrong, he adds, is not the last word: "that day will declare who is in the right and who in the wrong, when Christ appears, to the unspeakable consolation of the persecuted, and the everlasting confusion of their persecutors." The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott measures the stinted loaf and cup; Wesley measures the injustice and its reversal. Between them they show Micaiah bearing the prophet's ancient portion — the scorn, the prison, the meagre fare — and bearing it in the sure knowledge that the issue will vindicate him. Ahab means to return in peace and free his prisoner in triumph; the prophet knows he will not return at all.
27:
Micaiah stakes his whole prophetic standing on the outcome — "If thou certainly return in peace, then hath not the LORD spoken by me" — and turns from the king to the watching crowd: "Hearken, all ye people." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes that the words stand as in 1 Kings 22:28, and reads the closing summons as the prophet addressing the bystanders and making them witnesses to his prediction — calling the whole assembly to remember what he has said, that when Ahab fails to return they may know a true word was spoken. The phrase "Hearken, all ye people," he adds, is the very sentence that opens the book of the prophet Micah at Micah 1:2; some have thought Micaiah borrowed it thence, or that it stands here as a kind of abridgement of that whole book, though Ellicott, with the critic Thenius against such fancies, holds that the section before us bears indubitable marks of historical truth, and is probably an extract from the history of Jehoshaphat written by Jehu the son of Hanani, named at 2 Chronicles 20:34.

The prophet's challenge is the boldest a man can make: he offers his own credit as the test of God's word. If Ahab comes home safe, then Micaiah is a false prophet and may be treated as one; if Ahab does not, the people are to know that the LORD spoke by him and not by the four hundred. It is the confidence of a man who has stood in the heavenly council and has nothing to fear from the event. He does not plead against the prison or the bread of affliction; he simply appeals to the future, content to let the battle decide between him and his accusers.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marks this appeal as the abiding comfort of every persecuted servant of God: Micaiah, condemned to the prison and the bread and water of affliction, could yet with full assurance appeal to the issue, as all may do who are persecuted for their faithfulness. The day will declare who is in the right and who in the wrong. The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott secures the text, the summons to the witnesses, and the historical rootage of the whole narrative in Jehu's record; Henry draws the pastoral lesson. Between them they leave Micaiah where the chapter means him to stand — a solitary man led off to prison, having risked everything on a single event, and calling heaven and the whole people to mark whether the word of the LORD would stand. The armies will now settle it; and the prophet is willing.
28:
The warning delivered and the prophet jailed, the two kings march — "So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat the king of Judah went up to Ramoth-gilead" — and with that step the whole question raised in the council of heaven passes to the field for its answer. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the expedition as the tragic sequel to all that has gone before: Ahab goes up in the teeth of a plain prophecy, and drags his easy-natured ally with him. The good king Jehoshaphat, Henry observes, will expose himself in his royal robes and be endangered, yet delivered; the wicked Ahab will disguise himself, thinking to secure his life, and yet be slain — for no art and no arms can save those whom God has appointed to ruin, nor can any danger destroy those whom God will protect.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, in his survey of the chapter, sets the outcome plainly before the reader: both the kings go up against the Syrians, the confederate armies are defeated, and the king of Israel is slain. The march to Ramoth-gilead is thus the beginning of the end that Micaiah foretold. Every element of the coming disaster is already in place — the doom decreed above, the lying spirit sent forth, the king warned and unmoved, the true prophet silenced — and nothing remains but for the armies to move up and the word of the LORD to be fulfilled upon the mountains where the flock would be scattered. That two crowned heads should march to a battle already lost, one under sentence and the other under no obligation but a rash promise, is the very picture of men hurrying to accomplish, by their own free choice, the thing that God has spoken.

The witnesses do not divide. Henry frames the battle as the great demonstration that God governs the issue of war whatever men contrive; Clarke names the bare result. Between them they mark the solemn irony of the verse: that Jehoshaphat, who had asked to inquire at the word of the LORD, marches on after that word has been given and disregarded, bound by his rash pledge to a man under sentence of death. The two kings go up together — one to be spared by a mercy he scarcely deserved, the other to die by a decree he would not believe. And behind them, in the prison of Samaria, sits the one man who knew how the day would end, kept on bread and water "until the king return in peace" — a return that would never come.
29:
Ahab's battle-plan is a study in self-defeating cunning — "I will disguise myself, and will go to the battle; but put thou on thy robes." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott catches the breathless force of the Hebrew, "disguising myself and entering!" — a hurried, exclamatory way of speaking, as of a man improvising his own concealment on the eve of the fight. The following "they went" he notes as the chronicler's reading, where Kings has simply "he" — Ahab — "went into the battle," a variation several Hebrew manuscripts and all the ancient versions preserve. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke refers the disguise to his fuller comment at 1 Kings 22:30, where the stratagem is examined at length.

The arrangement bristles with suspicion, and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry does not spare it. Why should Ahab, having hidden his own royalty, urge his ally to march conspicuous in the robes that marked a king? Henry judges that Ahab, while pretending friendship, really aimed at Jehoshaphat's life, that he might have the managing of his son-in-law and successor; else he would never have advised him into the battle in his robes, which was but to make himself an easy mark for the enemy. If so, it was as unprincipled a piece of treachery as ever man was guilty of — and, as the sequel shows, Ahab was justly taken in the very pit he had digged for his friend, for the disguise he trusted would not save him, and the robes he thought would betray Jehoshaphat would not destroy the man God meant to spare. Whether or not the design against Jehoshaphat's life is pressed so far, the folly is plain: a king who has just heard his ruin decreed in heaven answers not with repentance but with a costume, seeking to slip through the battle unrecognized by men while forgetting that he cannot slip past the eye of God.

The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott fixes the hurried idiom and the textual variant; Clarke points to the deeper treatment of the ruse; Henry exposes the treachery beneath it. Between them they show the folly of a man who thought to outwit the word of God by a change of clothes. Ahab had heard that Israel would be scattered for want of its shepherd; he answers by hiding the shepherd, as though a doom pronounced in heaven could be dodged by a soldier's cloak. The disguise is the last refuge of a king who believed the prophecy enough to fear it, but not enough to repent of the war — and it is precisely the arrow shot "at a venture," heedless of disguises, that will find him out.
30:
The battle turns on a secret order in the Syrian camp — "Fight ye not with small or great, save only with the king of Israel." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes that the older account at 1 Kings 22:31 numbers these captains of the chariots as "thirty and two," a figure that looks back to the earlier Syrian wars of 1 Kings 20, which the chronicler has not paused to notice, though the Syriac and Arabic supply the number here; and he glosses "small or great" as our text has it, literally "with the small or the great." The command singles out one man in all the allied host: the Syrian king has resolved that the war shall be won or lost on the person of Ahab alone.

The order is at once sound strategy and unwitting instrument of prophecy. Benhadad, it seems, bore Ahab a personal grudge, or judged that with the king of Israel fallen the confederate armies would melt away; and so he bent his whole chariot-force upon finding and killing him. But the reader who has followed the chapter sees a deeper hand at work. Ahab has disguised himself precisely to escape notice, trusting that the enemy who seeks a king in royal robes will pass over a plain man in the press; and the Syrian command to spare all others and strike only at the king seems, on the face of it, exactly the danger his disguise was meant to foil. The two designs — the king's concealment and the enemy's single-minded search — are set against each other, and between them stands the decree of God, which will use the one to defeat the other.

Ellicott's care to recover the thirty-two captains from the parallel keeps the scale of the thing before us: not a stray archer but a whole squadron of chariot-commanders, all under one order, sweeping the field for one man. Yet the very concentration of the Syrian effort upon the king of Israel is what will spare Jehoshaphat and doom Ahab — for the captains, hunting a king, will first mistake the robed ally for their quarry, and then, undeceived, will turn from him to find the disguised king whom a random arrow has already marked. The secret order that meant to make the battle sure will serve, under God, only to make the prophecy sure. The command to "fight only with the king of Israel" is the enemy's plan; it is also, though Benhadad knows it not, the sentence of heaven seeking out its man.
31:
The Syrian captains, seeing a king in robes, fall upon the wrong man — "they said, It is the king of Israel. Therefore they compassed about him to fight: but Jehoshaphat cried out, and the LORD helped him; and God moved them to depart from him." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the cry and its answer as the chronicler's own theological signature. "Jehoshaphat cried out" — probably, in the first instance, to bring his own followers to the rescue, or to undeceive the enemy; but the words that follow, "the LORD helped him, and God moved them from him," Ellicott judges an addition from the chronicler's own pen, who understood the cry as a cry to God for help, a sense it often bears, and drove the captains away. The captains simply discovered their mistake and retired; and this perfectly natural event the chronicler regards as providential, and rightly so — for, as Ellicott finely puts it, Hebrew faith "knows nothing of an order of the world which can be separated even in thought from the constant personal activity of Jehovah."

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses read the deliverance the same way. Adam Clarke gives the Targum's version — "Jehoshaphat cried, and the Word of the LORD brought him assistance" — and John Wesley canvasses the cry's possible aims: to his friends for help, to his enemies to tell them he was not the king of Israel, or to God, "and not in vain; for he moved the captains to depart from him." Many, Wesley reflects, are moved in a manner unaccountable both to themselves and others, but an invisible power moves them. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry had drawn the same lesson: Jehoshaphat, when it was too late, wished himself in the habit of the poorest soldier; he cried to God for succour, and found it was not in vain, for the LORD helped him out of his distress by moving the captains to depart — God having all men's hearts in his hand, and turning them as he pleases, contrary to their own first intentions, to serve his purposes.

The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott traces the natural event and the faith that reads God in it; Clarke and Wesley and Henry all hear in the captains' turning the hand of an unseen mover. Between them they set the deliverance of Jehoshaphat over against the doom of Ahab as two sides of one providence: the king who wore his robes and should by every calculation have died is spared, because he cried to God; the king who hid himself and thought himself safe will fall, because God had marked him. The captains who compassed Jehoshaphat depart as unaccountably as they came — moved, the witnesses agree, by the same LORD who had heard a frightened king call upon his name in the middle of a battle he had no business fighting.
33:
The decree of heaven is executed by an archer who did not even know he was aiming at a king — "a certain man drew a bow at a venture, and smote the king of Israel between the joints of the harness." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott lingers over that phrase "at a venture." It means, he says, without design, as in the like expression at 2 Samuel 15:11, which Gesenius glosses "without thought of evil intent"; the Septuagint's "with good aim" he calls a bad guess, and prefers Rashi's explanation — the man drew his bow "without knowing why he chose that particular man to shoot at." The wound fell "between the joints of the harness," that is, at the opening of the breastplate; and here, Ellicott notes, the ancient versions only guess — the Syriac "between the division of his mail," the Vulgate "between the neck and shoulders" — none quite certain of the armour's anatomy, though all agree the arrow found the one unguarded seam.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reports the Targum's tradition, which will not leave the archer nameless: it makes him a captain of the Syrian host and sees in his random shot the appointed fulfilment of the words spoken against Ahab by the prophets, by Elijah before and by Micaiah the son of Imla now, the arrow finding the king between the heart and the caul of the liver where the coat of mail was joined. Whether or not the name be pressed, the point of the tradition is sound — that the shaft loosed without aim was aimed by another hand, and that the prophecies which the king had jailed and starved a man for speaking were now coming true upon his own body.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse gathers the whole chapter into a single stroke. Ellicott unfolds the language of chance; Clarke presses the hidden purpose behind it. Ahab had disguised himself to escape just such a death; but the arrow drawn "at a venture" cared nothing for disguises, and slipped through the one gap in his armour as though guided to it. What the bowman did blindly, God did deliberately. The king who trusted four hundred prophets and hid from the word of the one is struck down by a chance arrow that was no chance at all — the flock's shepherd smitten, as Micaiah had foreseen, so that Israel should be scattered on the mountains. And the cry that follows, "carry me out of the host, for I am wounded," is the beginning of the end the council of heaven had decreed and the disguise could not avert.
34:
The chapter ends with a dying king propping himself upright so that his army may not know he is slain — "the battle increased that day: howbeit the king of Israel stayed himself up in his chariot against the Syrians until the even; and about the time of the sun going down he died." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders "increased" as "went up, grew," like the springing growth of the vine at Genesis 40:10, and reads the picture of Ahab literally: he "continued holding himself up in the chariot, facing Aram, until the evening." The chronicler's reading, he judges, is preferable to that of Kings — the sense being that Ahab bravely bore up against the pain of his wound in order not to discourage his own side by quitting the field. And Ellicott marks a telling omission: the rest of the older narrative, the return of the routed army and the washing of Ahab's chariot at the pool of Samaria, told at 1 Kings 22:36-38, the chronicler leaves out, because Jehoshaphat had no part in it, and perhaps because he perceived that the real climax of this vivid old story is the death of the king at sundown, and would let the tale close there.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke honours the soldier even while he weighs the sinner. There was a great deal of true personal courage and patriotism, he says, in this last act of the king of Israel: Ahab knew that if his troops learned he was mortally wounded they would give way and the slaughter in the rout would be terrible, and so he held himself up till evening should of itself close the battle. Only when he died did the Israelites find their king slain and leave the field to their foes; and had it not been for this wound, Clarke thinks, the Syrians had probably been defeated. Above all he presses the lesson the whole chapter has been teaching about the lying spirit: the reader should never forget a truth so frequently occurring in Scripture, that God is repeatedly represented as doing what, in the course of his providence, he only permits to be done.

The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott fixes the dying king's posture and the chronicler's deliberate close; Clarke admires the courage and draws the doctrine. Between them they let the chapter end where it must — with Ahab slain at the setting of the sun, exactly as Micaiah had foreseen, the shepherd struck and the flock scattered. The four hundred had cried "Go up and prosper"; the one had said "I saw all Israel scattered upon the mountains"; and the sun goes down on the proof of which had spoken for God. The king who jailed the prophet and left him bread and water "until I return in peace" does not return at all, and the word of the LORD, risked upon the event, stands vindicated over the body of the man who would not hear it.
